item.title: Counting Caffeine Molecules and Atoms by Mass
item.stimulus:
A tablet of a caffeine supplement contains 0.200 g of caffeine, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂. The molar mass of caffeine is 194.19 g/mol, and Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Answer the following. Report each calculated answer with units and an appropriate number of significant digits.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of caffeine in the tablet.

criteria.evidence: Response converts the 0.200 g mass to moles using the molar mass 194.19 g/mol and reports 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol.
criteria.fix: Use n = m/M: divide the mass in grams by the molar mass in g/mol, keeping three significant digits from 0.200 g.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of caffeine molecules in the tablet.

criteria.evidence: Response converts the amount of caffeine to a number of molecules with Avogadro's number (for example 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) and reports 6.20 × 10²⁰ molecules, or a value consistent with the student's answer to the previous part.
criteria.fix: Multiply the amount in moles by Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³ per mole, to turn moles into a count of molecules.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of nitrogen atoms in the caffeine in the tablet.

criteria.text: Calculates 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms, using 4 nitrogen atoms per caffeine molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the subscript 4 for N in C₈H₁₀N₄O₂ and reports 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms, or 4 times the student's number of molecules from the previous part.
criteria.fix: Read the element's subscript in the formula and multiply the number of molecules by that subscript to count its atoms.

parts.prompt: The average mass of one caffeine molecule is 194.19 amu. Calculate the average mass of one caffeine molecule in grams.

criteria.text: Calculates 3.225 × 10⁻²² g for the mass of one caffeine molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a valid conversion, such as dividing 194.19 g/mol by 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol, and reports 3.225 × 10⁻²² g; a difference in the last digit caused by a rounded conversion factor is acceptable.
criteria.fix: The amu mass of one molecule equals the grams in one mole, so divide the molar mass by Avogadro's number to get grams per molecule.

item.model_answer:
(a) n = m/M = 0.200 g ÷ 194.19 g/mol = 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol of caffeine.

(b) Number of molecules = 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 6.20 × 10²⁰ caffeine molecules.

(c) Each caffeine molecule, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, contains 4 nitrogen atoms. Number of N atoms = 4 × 6.20 × 10²⁰ = 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms.

(d) Because the average mass of one molecule in amu is numerically equal to the molar mass in grams, 1 mol of caffeine (6.022 × 10²³ molecules) has a mass of 194.19 g. Mass of one molecule = 194.19 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 3.225 × 10⁻²² g.
item.verification_python:
import math
NA=6.022e23
M=194.19
m=0.200
# molar mass check from atomic masses (given value is standard)
assert abs((8*12.011+10*1.008+4*14.007+2*15.999)-M)<0.02
n=m/M
assert abs(n-1.03e-3)<0.005e-3
N=n*NA
assert abs(N-6.20e20)<0.005e20
assert abs(1.03e-3*NA-6.20e20)<0.005e20
NN=4*N
assert abs(NN-2.48e21)<0.005e21
assert abs(4*6.20e20-2.48e21)<1e17
mm=M/NA
assert abs(mm-3.225e-22)<0.0005e-22
assert abs(194.19*1.66054e-24-3.225e-22)<0.001e-22
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Counting Particles in Weighed Water and Copper Samples
item.stimulus:
A student uses an analytical balance to measure out a sample of liquid water and a piece of pure copper wire. The data are shown below. Use the molar masses H = 1.008 g/mol, O = 16.00 g/mol, Cu = 63.55 g/mol and Avogadro's number NA = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Measurement | Mass (g)
Empty beaker | 48.217
Beaker + water | 57.223
Copper wire | 3.178
item.model_answer:
(a) Mass of water = 57.223 g − 48.217 g = 9.006 g. Molar mass of H2O = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. n = m/M = 9.006 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.4998 mol H2O.

(b) 0.4998 mol H2O × (6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol) × (2 H atoms/molecule) = 6.019 × 10²³ H atoms.

(c) n = 3.178 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol = 0.05001 mol Cu. 0.05001 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol = 3.011 × 10²² Cu atoms.

(d) The claim is incorrect. The ratio of particles equals the ratio of moles: 0.4998 mol ÷ 0.05001 mol ≈ 9.99, so the water contains about 10 times as many H2O molecules as the wire contains Cu atoms, not 2.8 times. The mass ratio and particle ratio differ because the particles have different masses. One Cu atom has an average mass of 63.55 amu, while one H2O molecule has a mass of 18.02 amu, so each Cu atom is about 3.5 times as massive. Therefore a gram of copper contains about 3.5 times fewer particles than a gram of water, and 2.8 × 3.5 ≈ 10.
item.verification_python:
import math
NA=6.022e23
H=1.008;O=16.00;Cu=63.55
m_w=57.223-48.217
assert abs(m_w-9.006)<1e-9
M_w=2*H+O
assert abs(M_w-18.016)<1e-9
n_w=m_w/18.02
assert abs(n_w-0.4998)<5e-5
n_w2=m_w/M_w
assert abs(n_w2-0.4999)<5e-5
H_atoms=n_w*2*NA
assert abs(H_atoms/1e23-6.019)<5e-4
H_atoms2=n_w2*2*NA
assert 6.019<=round(H_atoms2/1e23,3)<=6.021
n_cu=3.178/Cu
assert abs(n_cu-0.05001)<5e-6
cu_atoms=n_cu*NA
assert abs(cu_atoms/1e22-3.011)<5e-4
mass_ratio=m_w/3.178
assert abs(mass_ratio-2.8)<0.05
ratio=n_w/n_cu
assert abs(ratio-9.99)<0.01
assert abs(0.4998/0.05001-9.99)<0.01
pm=Cu/18.02
assert abs(pm-3.5)<0.05
assert abs(2.8*3.5-10)<0.3
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

criteria.text: Moles of H2O = 0.4998 mol, from water mass 9.006 g divided by molar mass 18.02 g/mol
criteria.evidence: Response subtracts to get 9.006 g of water, uses a molar mass of 18.02 g/mol (or 18.016 g/mol), applies n = m/M, and reports about 0.4998 mol (0.4999 mol if 18.016 is used) to 4 significant figures.
criteria.fix: Subtract the empty beaker mass first, build the molar mass from the formula H2O, then divide mass by molar mass using n = m/M.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms in the water sample.

criteria.text: Number of H atoms = 6.019 × 10²³, using 2 H atoms per H2O molecule and Avogadro's number
criteria.evidence: Response multiplies moles of H2O (from part (a)) by 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol and by 2 H atoms per molecule, giving about 6.019 × 10²³ H atoms (values from 6.019 to 6.021 × 10²³ accepted; consistent with an answer carried from part (a)).
criteria.fix: After converting moles to molecules with Avogadro's number, multiply by the subscript to count atoms of that element per molecule.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of copper atoms in the copper wire.

criteria.text: Number of Cu atoms = 3.011 × 10²² from 3.178 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol = 0.05001 mol, times NA
criteria.evidence: Response converts 3.178 g Cu to 0.05001 mol using 63.55 g/mol, then multiplies by 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol to get 3.011 × 10²² Cu atoms with 4 significant figures.
criteria.fix: Convert grams to moles with the molar mass, then multiply moles by 6.022 × 10²³ to get the particle count.

parts.prompt: The water sample has about 2.8 times the mass of the copper wire. A classmate claims that the water sample therefore contains about 2.8 times as many particles (H2O molecules) as the copper wire contains Cu atoms. Evaluate the claim using your results, and explain at the particle level why mass ratio and particle ratio differ.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect: the water contains about 10 times (≈9.99 times) as many molecules as the wire has Cu atoms
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and supports it with a ratio of moles or particles, such as 0.4998 mol ÷ 0.05001 mol ≈ 10 (consistent with earlier answers).
criteria.fix: Compare particle counts by dividing moles of one sample by moles of the other, not by comparing masses.

criteria.text: Explains that each Cu atom (63.55 amu) is about 3.5 times as massive as an H2O molecule (18.02 amu), so a gram of copper contains fewer particles
criteria.evidence: Response connects the average mass of one particle in amu (numerically equal to molar mass) to the conclusion that heavier particles mean fewer particles per unit mass, so equal or similar masses do not contain equal numbers of particles.
criteria.fix: Compare the mass of one particle of each substance in amu and state that heavier particles give fewer particles per gram.

item.title: Moles, Molecules, and Atoms in a Sugar Cube
item.stimulus:
A student weighs a single sugar cube made of pure sucrose, C12H22O11, and records a mass of 2.84 g. The student wants to connect this measured mass to the number of particles in the cube. Use the atomic masses in the table below and Avogadro's number, NA = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Element | Average atomic mass (amu)
C | 12.01
H | 1.008
O | 16.00
item.model_answer:
(a) M(C12H22O11) = 12(12.01) + 22(1.008) + 11(16.00) = 144.12 + 22.176 + 176.00 = 342.30 g/mol. n = m/M = 2.84 g ÷ 342.30 g/mol = 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol sucrose.

(b) O atoms = (8.30 × 10⁻³ mol sucrose) × (11 mol O / 1 mol sucrose) × (6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol) = 5.50 × 10²² oxygen atoms.

(c) Because the mass of one molecule in amu equals the molar mass in grams, one mole of sucrose has a mass of 342.30 g. Mass of one molecule = 342.30 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 5.684 × 10⁻²² g.

(d) The water sample contains more molecules. Each water molecule has a much smaller mass than a sucrose molecule (18.02 g/mol compared with 342.30 g/mol), so the same 2.84 g of water corresponds to more moles: 2.84 g ÷ 18.02 g/mol = 0.158 mol H2O, compared with 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol sucrose. More moles means more molecules, since each mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
item.verification_python:
import math
C,H,O=12.01,1.008,16.00
M=12*C+22*H+11*O
assert abs(M-342.296)<1e-6
assert abs(round(M,2)-342.30)<1e-9
NA=6.022e23
n=2.84/342.30
assert abs(n-8.30e-3)<0.005e-3
O_atoms=n*11*NA
assert abs(O_atoms-5.50e22)<0.005e22
m1=342.30/NA
assert abs(m1-5.684e-22)<0.0005e-22
nw=2.84/18.02
assert abs(nw-0.158)<0.0005
Mw=2*H+O
assert abs(Mw-18.016)<1e-9
assert nw>n
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

criteria.evidence: Response sums atomic masses (12 × 12.01 + 22 × 1.008 + 11 × 16.00 ≈ 342.3 g/mol), divides 2.84 g by this molar mass, and reports 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol with units and 3 significant figures
criteria.fix: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript, add them for molar mass, then use n = m/M and keep three significant figures.
